title: Routing algorithms and protocols
subtitle: How routers learn the cheapest path: by knowing the whole map, or by asking their neighbours.

sections.title: Forwarding versus routing
sections.body: Forwarding is the per-packet act of looking up the destination in the forwarding table and choosing the output port — fast, done in hardware. Routing is the slower process that builds that table. Routes can be static (configured by hand) or dynamic (learned by a routing protocol). Within an organisation routers use an interior protocol (RIP, OSPF, EIGRP); between organisations the Internet uses the exterior protocol BGP.

questions.prompt: Which is done for every packet?

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: Running Dijkstra per packet would be far too slow.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Routing runs in the background updating the table.

sections.title: Link state: Dijkstra
sections.body: In link-state routing (OSPF) every router floods the state of its links, so all routers hold the same map, then each runs Dijkstra’s algorithm to find least-cost paths from itself. Repeatedly settle the nearest unsettled node and relax its neighbours. On the textbook graph from node u the costs to v, x, w, y, z come out as 2, 1, 3, 2, 4; the route to z is u→x→y→z.

questions.prompt: Dijkstra’s algorithm requires that link costs be…

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: A negative edge could make an already-settled node cheaper to reach later.

problems.answer: D(v)=2, D(x)=1, D(w)=3 (via x, y), D(y)=2, D(z)=4 via u→x→y→z.

sections.title: Distance vector: Bellman–Ford
sections.body: In distance-vector routing (RIP) each router knows only its links and its neighbours’ tables. Periodically it recomputes D(i,j) = min over neighbours k of [cost(i,k) + D(k,j)]. Information spreads one hop per round, and the tables converge to the same answers as Dijkstra. Problems: slow convergence and the count-to-infinity problem when a link fails, mitigated by split horizon and a small maximum hop count (RIP: 15).

choices.text: After a failure, routers keep advertising stale routes to each other and the cost climbs slowly.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Each router believes a neighbour’s outdated offer; it takes many rounds to give up.

sections.title: RIP, OSPF, EIGRP, BGP
sections.body: RIP: distance vector, hop count, 15 max. OSPF: link state, areas, fast convergence. EIGRP: Cisco’s advanced distance vector. BGP: path-vector between autonomous systems; it is policy-driven, not cost-driven. Supporting protocols: ARP maps IP to MAC on a link; ICMP reports errors and powers ping/traceroute.

choices.text: Maps an IP address to a MAC address on the local link.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Frames need a MAC destination even though packets carry IP.

sections.title: Congestion and traffic shaping
sections.body: When offered load exceeds capacity, queues grow and packets are dropped. Control can be open-loop (traffic shaping with a leaky bucket or token bucket) or closed-loop (feedback such as TCP’s window, next lesson). A token bucket lets bursts through up to its depth, then enforces the average rate.

worked.why: A token bucket adds tokens at 100 packets/s and holds at most 50. The source bursts.
It can send 50 packets at once, then 100 per second sustained.

questions.prompt: A leaky bucket smooths traffic by…

choices.text: Releasing packets at a constant rate whatever the input burstiness.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: That is the token bucket (up to its depth).

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
• Forwarding = lookup; routing = table building.
  • Link state: full map + Dijkstra. Distance vector: neighbours’ tables + Bellman–Ford.
  • BGP glues autonomous systems together by policy.
